title: Berth: coins that build apps
intro: Most token launches sell a promise and a chart. Berth sells a product. You write one sentence describing an app. A coin launches on pump.fun. Its trading fees become a build budget that pays an AI agent to design, build, deploy and keep iterating on that app. The app then charges real users, and 85% of everything it earns buys the coin back on the open market and burns it. Nobody is ever paid a distribution; supply just falls.

This is the whole idea in one line: fees fund the build, revenue funds the burn. The front page ranks coins by the dollars their product actually earned, not by volume or market cap. What follows is exactly how that works end to end, why an app you prompted into existence can't drain your wallet, and what has already been verified running in production.

ps: You don't write code. You write the idea. Your prompt is first moderated, then turned into a concrete spec: what the app does, who pays for it, the MVP feature list, and the price. You approve that spec, and it gets pinned to the coin page, so buyers are funding something specific rather than a vibe.

Then a refundable 0.05 SOL stake launches the coin on pump.fun through a per-app keypair that is also the coin's fee creator. The stake is spam control; it comes back to you the moment your coin funds its first build. From that point on, the machine takes over and the app builds itself.

sections.h: The money: two streams, one direction
ps: Every coin has two independent money streams, and both are pointed at the product. Creator (trading) fees split three ways: 60% into the app's build budget, 25% into the $BERTH platform-coin buyback, and 15% to you, the launcher.

App revenue splits differently: 85% buys back and burns the app's own coin, 10% goes to $BERTH, and 5% covers platform operations. There is no dividend, no yield, and no revenue share. A buyback here is a burn: the platform buys tokens on the open market and destroys them.

Half of the 60% build cut is a per-coin credits slice that is swept from SOL to USDC to the card that pays the model bill, so a coin's own fees fund its own compute. A coin that earned nothing gets no compute, and one coin's balance can never be spent by another.

sections.h: The build loop, behind a gate
ps: The first build starts once a coin has accrued $50 of build budget. A fresh E2B microVM boots, and an agent driving the Claude Agent SDK works against a fixed, audited template. Every step it takes, every note, tool call, commit and test, streams live to the coin page as a public build log.

Nothing reaches users until it passes the gate: npm run build, a Playwright smoke test, screenshots, a Lighthouse audit, and a reviewer agent that reads the diff and blocks anything unsafe or off-spec. On approval it commits, pushes and deploys, and the budget is debited by the job's actual metered cost, not a flat fee. Later iterations run from $10 of budget and follow the roadmap holders voted for.

sections.h: Why a prompted app can't drain a wallet
ps: This is the question that matters, and the answer is architecture, not a promise. The agent never writes auth, wallet or payment code. Those are platform-hosted and reached only through @berth/app-sdk, so the model literally cannot hand-roll a transfer or touch a key.

On top of that, generated apps run under a strict content-security policy with no outbound network, banned raw fetch/eval/external scripts, and server logic executes in a QuickJS sandbox capped at 64MB and a 5-second deadline. A reviewer agent gates every single deploy, and all app source is public and MIT, so you can read exactly what runs.

Anyone can claim revenue; Berth makes it checkable. The platform is the merchant of record, so every USDC checkout, subscription and x402 per-call payment is verified on-chain by signature and memo before it is ever counted as revenue.

When enough revenue accumulates, the executor buys the coin back and burns it, and each burn's memo carries a sha256 of the exact revenue-event ids it settles. That means the path from a payment to a destroyed token is reproducible by anyone: pull the swap and the burn, hash the ids, and you get the same string. It's a receipt, not a claim.

sections.h: Ranked by what the product earned
ps: The front page does not rank by volume, market cap, or how loud a launch was. It ranks coins by the dollars their app collected from real users. A coin whose product earns money rises; a coin with a chart and no product does not.

Every coin page then shows the same thing at three depths: is it making money, is it being built, and can I verify it, backed by the live money block, the streaming build log, and the full burn ledger with its attestation.
$BERTH is the coin the platform itself runs on. It has exactly two inflows, 25% of every app's creator fees and 10% of every app's revenue, and two one-way sinks.

The first sink is buyback-and-burn: the treasury balance is swapped for $BERTH and the tokens are destroyed. The second is staking to boost: holders stake $BERTH against a specific app to move it to the front of the build queue and earn that app's staker fee share while staked, and can unstake at any time. Neither sink pays or promises anything to holders.

sections.h: When a coin runs out of budget
ps: Budget hitting zero does not kill an app. It goes dormant: the live app keeps serving traffic and keeps earning revenue, and only the build loop pauses. It sits behind a buy-to-revive page, and any new trading fee or a direct top-up restarts it. Nothing is abandoned; it just waits for fuel.

Berth is engineered like infrastructure. As of go-live: 211 tests pass with no network access, the feature matrix is 50 of 53 (the three gaps are funding-only), the security perimeter scores 31 pass and 0 fail against the live API, and the reconcile pass reports 0 drift across jobs, sandboxes, tokens, the ledger and uncollected fees.

A real build pipeline already runs end to end in production: the sandbox boots, the template lands, install and build and the Playwright smoke test pass, screenshots and the Lighthouse audit run, and the reviewer's policy gate evaluates the diff. It stops at exactly one place, the model credit balance. In the interest of honesty, Berth is at its starting line, and the screenshots in this article use representative data to show the interface, not revenue already earned.

closing: berth.fun. Fees fund the build. Revenue funds the burn. Every generated app is MIT; launchers assign no IP and receive no equity or supply. Coins are not investments, apps can fail, and nothing here is financial advice.
